prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "HOME DEPOT, INC." (ticker HD), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "HD", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The Home Depot, Inc.
result.industry: Home improvement retail and specialty building-products distribution
markets: US, Canada and Mexico home improvement retail (DIY and do-it-for-me homeowners)
Professional contractor supply (Pro customers, trade credit, delivery)
Specialty trade distribution via SRS and GMS (roofing, drywall/interior products, landscape, pool)

mission.plain: Home Depot says it aims to give the best service to its customers, associates, communities and shareholders, guided by its customer-first 'inverted pyramid' values; it does not publish a formal one-line mission statement on its About Us page.

about.plain: Home Depot runs huge orange warehouse stores that sell everything needed to build, fix or decorate a home: wood, paint, tools, plumbing, lights, appliances and garden plants. It has 2,359 stores in the US, Canada and Mexico and also sells online. It also owns SRS, a company that delivers roofing, drywall, pool and landscape supplies straight to builders and contractors. Customers can also hire it to install things like floors, windows and water heaters.
about.customers: Homeowners doing their own projects, and professional builders, remodelers, roofers, electricians and plumbers who buy supplies for their jobs.
about.everyday: If your family ever bought paint, a lawnmower, a light bulb or lumber for a fence, there's a good chance it came from the orange Home Depot store down the road.

money.plain: Lumber, tools, paint, plumbing, electrical, appliances, flooring, garden
Bulk building materials, jobsite delivery, Pro Xtra loyalty and trade credit
Roofing, drywall, ceilings, steel framing, pool and landscape supplies delivered to contractors from over 1,250 branches
Paid installation of flooring, water heaters, windows and more
Magic Apron assistant, Blueprint Takeoffs and Material List Builder for project planning

result.summary: Home Depot has a wide moat built on scale: as the largest home improvement retailer it buys more cheaply, runs a dense store-and-distribution network and carries a much broader Pro assortment than smaller rivals, which supports operating margins (12.7% in FY2025) above Lowe's (11.8%). The SRS and GMS acquisitions extend that scale into contractor distribution. The advantage is durable but cyclical: sales depend on housing turnover and remodeling, and comparable sales have been roughly flat since 2023.

pricingPower.evidence: Gross margin has held in a tight 33.3%-34.0% band from FY2020 to FY2025 through inflation and tariffs, and in FY2025 comparable average ticket rose 1.4% while comparable transactions fell 1.0%, showing it can pass on costs but not push volume; much of its range (lumber, commodities) is price-transparent and matched against Lowe's and online sellers.

moats.evidence: The orange 'Home Depot' brand is the best-known name in US home improvement, and exclusive brands such as Husky, Ryobi and Milwaukee tool partnerships draw traffic, but many products are national brands also sold by Lowe's and Amazon.

DIY shoppers can easily switch stores; Pro customers face some friction through Pro Xtra loyalty, trade credit accounts and SRS delivery relationships, but contractors still shop on price and availability.
One more shopper does not make the store more valuable to others; there is no meaningful network effect.

With $164.7B of FY2025 sales, almost twice Lowe's $86.3B, Home Depot spreads buying, distribution, technology and advertising over a far larger base, earning a 12.7% operating margin and roughly 20% return on invested capital.
The US big-box home improvement market is effectively a duopoly with Lowe's; most local markets can support only one or two 100,000-square-foot stores, which deters new entrants.
Its model is the incumbent model; no evidence that rivals are unable to copy it for fear of hurting their own business.

Decades of supply-chain investment (flatbed distribution centers, FDC Relay delivery, about 50% of US online orders fulfilled through stores) and merchandising know-how are hard for smaller chains to match.
It holds strong store real estate and exclusive brand deals, but no truly exclusive resource competitors cannot access.

customers.evidence: Home Depot typically scores at or near the top of the home improvement category in the American Customer Satisfaction Index, but comparable customer transactions fell 1.0% in FY2025 and comparable sales were only +0.3%, so loyalty is solid rather than exceptional.

talent.evidence: About 472,400 associates at FY2025 year-end; its 'orange-blooded' servant-leadership culture and Success Sharing bonuses for hourly staff are well regarded, but it is a large retail employer with high front-line turnover rather than a top employer-ranking name.

product.evidence: It offers the broadest in-stock home improvement assortment in North America across 2,359 stores plus SRS's 1,250+ branches, with exclusive brands such as Ryobi and Husky and strong Pro fulfilment, generally regarded as the category leader ahead of Lowe's.

competitors.name: Lowe's Companies
competitors.note: The other national big-box home improvement chain; competes on nearly every DIY and Pro product, and owns FBM and ADG in Pro distribution.

competitors.name: Menards
competitors.note: Private Midwest home improvement chain competing directly on lumber, tools and DIY.

competitors.name: QXO (Beacon)
competitors.note: Owns Beacon, the largest rival to SRS in roofing and building-products distribution.

competitors.name: Builders FirstSource
competitors.note: Lumber, trusses, windows and millwork supplied to professional homebuilders.

competitors.name: Floor & Decor
competitors.note: Specialty hard-surface flooring stores competing with Home Depot's flooring department.

competitors.name: Amazon.com
competitors.note: Online tools, hardware, smart-home, lighting and home goods.

competitors.name: Walmart
competitors.note: Basic hardware, paint, garden and seasonal goods.

competitors.name: Tractor Supply
competitors.note: Rural lifestyle stores overlapping in outdoor power equipment, fencing and garden.

competitors.name: Ace Hardware
competitors.note: Retailer-owned cooperative of neighbourhood hardware stores competing on convenience.

competitors.name: Harbor Freight Tools
competitors.note: Private discount tool chain competing on hand and power tools.

competitors.name: Sherwin-Williams
competitors.note: Paint stores serving professional painters, competing with Home Depot's paint department.

competitors.name: Ferguson Enterprises
competitors.note: Plumbing, HVAC and waterworks distribution to contractors.

competitors.name: Wayfair
competitors.note: Online furniture, decor, lighting and some home improvement items.

marketShare.market: North American home improvement (Home Depot's own ~$1.1 trillion total addressable market definition, Dec 2025)
marketShare.measure: revenue (company sales divided by the ~$1.1T TAM; rough, as rivals' sales include some non-home-improvement items)

threats: Prolonged housing freeze: 30-year mortgage rates reached 7.28% on Oct 1, 2026, depressing home sales and big-ticket remodeling; comparable sales were only +0.3% in FY2025.
Lowe's pushing harder into Pro distribution (FBM, ADG acquisitions) and QXO consolidating building-products distribution against SRS.
Integration risk and lower returns from the $18.25B SRS and $5.5B GMS acquisitions, which raised debt to about $52.9B and paused buybacks.
Amazon and other online sellers taking share in tools, hardware, lighting and decor.
Tariffs and input-cost inflation squeezing gross margin, and leadership uncertainty while CEO Ted Decker is on medical leave (since Aug 2026).

ceo.name: Ted (Edward P.) Decker
ceo.background: BA in English, College of William & Mary; MBA, Carnegie Mellon; earlier finance and strategy roles at PNC, Scott Paper and Kimberly-Clark; joined Home Depot in 2000 and ran merchandising (2014-2020) and was President/COO (2020-2022). On temporary medical leave since Aug 2026, with Ann-Marie Campbell and CFO Richard McPhail running the office of the CEO.

c1.evidence: Home Depot leads a mature, slow-growing industry: FY2025 sales rose 3.2% to $164.7B and comparable sales just 0.3%, not an emerging fast-growth market.

c2.evidence: Customers choose it for the broadest in-stock assortment, Pro services and convenience across 2,359 stores, a scale advantage that is durable, but Lowe's offers a very similar proposition.

c3.evidence: The orange Home Depot brand is a household name and the default leader in US home improvement, nearly twice the size of Lowe's by sales.

c4.evidence: Management constantly emphasises its customer-first 'inverted pyramid' values and servant leadership, but there is no published mission beyond excellent service, and its purpose is commercial rather than world-changing.

c6.evidence: “orange, big-box, DIY, everything for the house” — the impression is mostly positive, as a reliable, well-stocked place to buy tools and materials, though some complain about thin in-store staffing.

c7.evidence: Its addressable market is large (about $1.1 trillion by the company's estimate) and supported by an aging US housing stock, but it grows roughly with housing and the economy rather than riding a powerful secular trend.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into the larger Pro and specialty-distribution market through SRS ($18.25B, 2024) and GMS ($5.5B, 2025) plus about 80 new stores planned, but remains tied to home improvement.

m1.evidence: Ted Decker has set a clear strategy to win the complex Pro customer and build an interconnected, AI-assisted shopping experience, but it is an evolution rather than a bold new vision.

m2.evidence: Decker is a 25-year company lifer who thinks long-term (multi-year Pro and supply-chain build-outs), but he is a professional manager, not a founder.

m4.evidence: Home Depot's culture is explicitly built on the inverted pyramid, with customers and front-line associates on top and the CEO at the bottom, and Decker regularly reinforces this.

m5.evidence: The strong 'orange-blooded' culture was built by founders Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank; under Decker it has added AI tools such as Magic Apron, but it is not an inventor of new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: Decker is a hands-on merchant who ran merchandising for six years, but his background is English and finance, not engineering.

m7.evidence: Decker has a reputation for integrity and the company backs causes like the Home Depot Foundation's veterans housing work, but nothing suggests stewardship beyond being a responsible corporate leader.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Ted Decker giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Decker is a low-key, understated executive rather than a famous, distinctive public personality.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2022, sales grew from $157.4B (FY2022) to $164.7B (FY2025) largely via acquisitions, while operating margin fell from 15.3% to 12.7% and diluted EPS from $16.69 to $14.23, in a weak housing market.

m10.evidence: Home Depot is known for disciplined cost control and capital allocation ('Smarter Investments, Richer Returns'), but not for Bezos-style frugality.

c10.evidence: It helps millions of households in the US, Canada and Mexico repair and improve their homes, but it does not operate worldwide or transform lives the way global platforms do.

p2.evidence: Running a 2,359-store supply chain with 470,000 associates is operationally hard and useful, but selling building materials is not extremely hard to do.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in four of the last five years (FY2021 +14.4%, FY2022 +4.1%, FY2024 +4.5%, FY2025 +3.2%) but fell 3.0% in FY2023 to $152.7B.

f2.evidence: Gross margin slipped from 33.95% in FY2020 to 33.32% in FY2025, and operating margin fell from a 15.3% peak in FY2022 to 12.7% in FY2025.

f3.evidence: At Aug 2, 2026 total debt was about $52.9B against just $2.1B of cash, roughly 3.2 times FY2025 operating cash flow of $16.3B, though shareholders' equity is positive at $16.6B.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $18.3B (FY2020) to $20.9B (FY2025) but has fallen every year since its $24.0B FY2022 peak; operating cash flow was $16.3B in FY2025 versus $16.6B in FY2021.

v1.evidence: Home Depot is the category leader with the widest in-stock assortment and best Pro offering, but Lowe's is a close substitute for most shoppers, so there is no overwhelming reason to choose it everywhere.

v2.evidence: Its culture and Success Sharing bonuses are well regarded and it appears on lists such as Forbes' large employer rankings, but it is not usually among the very top 'best places to work'.

c5.evidence: If it vanished, millions of homeowners and contractors would lose their go-to source for tools and materials and face higher prices and longer trips, though Lowe's, Menards and distributors would fill much of the gap.
